source: Zito-Wolf (1991) Book review of Minton, Learning Search Control Knowledge (Machine Learning 6:197-204)
finding: Secondary read of what Minton measured in PRODIGY/EBL. Learned control rules were monitored at run time. A rule was dropped if its match cost exceeded its estimated savings. Utility = average search saved minus cost of using the rule.
numbers: About 20% of generated rules were kept. Speed-up factor 2-3 on all problems in 3 domains (block stacking, robot-and-rooms, job-shop scheduling). Phases: learn, settle (utility evaluation), test. Dropping compression or utility evaluation each hurt a lot.
limits: This is a book review, not Minton's chapter or thesis tables. Minton 1990 chapter itself not obtained. The review notes the utility monitor can mis-rate good rules when bad rules dilute their savings.
agent_relevance: The utility problem is a measured fact for rule learners: keep about one in five, and judge each by saved effort minus use cost. For LLM case banks the cost term is context tokens and distraction, and the savings term is accuracy gain. It supports a retain test that charges each case its prompt cost.

source: Minton (1991) Reply to Zito-Wolf's review (Machine Learning 6:205-206)
finding: Minton says the overall speed-ups look modest because he capped solve time. Without the cap, the no-learning solver would hit exponential blow-ups on large problems. Learning from failure was usually more useful than learning from success in his tests, but he says this is not a general law.
numbers: Without domain-dependent axioms in compression, blocksworld performance after learning fell about 30%, still better than no learning. One third of learned rules used those axioms; they shrank by 19% on average. Test problems of increasing maximum size, some later ones actually smaller.
quote: the primary contribution of the book is the description of the utility problem and techniques for dealing with the utility problem
limits: Author's own caveat: constant time bound hides the asymptotic effect; problem difficulty did not strictly rise. Tables from the thesis are not in the book.
agent_relevance: Measured speed-ups depend on the test setup. Any LLM maintenance test must state its budget and problem mix. Also supports keeping failure-derived knowledge (compare ReasoningBank).

source: Ram and Leake (1995) Goal-Driven Learning, introduction (MIT Press, in-press draft)
finding: The only Francis and Ram 1993 item found is a reference line: Computational Models of the Utility Problem and their Application to a Utility Analysis of Case-Based Reasoning (ML-93 workshop). The draft cites it, with Minton 1990, as support for deciding what to learn by utility analysis.
numbers: No numbers. Francis and Ram 1993 text itself was not found online.
limits: Citation only. Gap 10 stays half open: Minton is now read second-hand (d01, d02); Francis and Ram is not read.
agent_relevance: Utility analysis of CBR is old, but no free source gives its swamping numbers. Do not quote numbers for it.

source: Wei et al. (2026) Evo-Memory: Benchmarking LLM Agent Test-time Learning with Self-Evolving Memory
finding: A benchmark of 10+ memory methods, on single-turn reasoning (AIME 24/25, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, ToolBench) and multi-turn embodied tasks, with Gemini 2.5 (Flash, Flash-Lite, Pro) and Claude (3.5 Haiku, 3.7 Sonnet). All methods share one retriever (bge-base) and top-4 retrieval and one prompt-length limit. Simple retrieval of raw experience (ExpRAG) is a strong baseline. Gains on single-turn reasoning are moderate.
numbers: Single-turn, Gemini 2.5 Flash: ReMem (with a Prune/Refine step) average exact match 0.65; ExpRAG about equal. On Claude 3.7 Sonnet the single-turn averages run only 0.48-0.59 across methods (Mem0 lowest, 0.49; baseline 0.54, history 0.55). Multi-turn Claude 3.7: ReMem 0.92 success on AlfWorld vs ExpRAG 0.74, ExpRecent 0.66. Gain correlates with within-dataset task similarity, Pearson r 0.717 (Gemini Flash), 0.563 (Claude 3.7). Pruning drops 36.8% of memories on GPQA, 17.5% and 10.8% on AIME 24/25. With failed experiences stored without filter, baselines degrade; ReMem stays robust (Table 3, AlfWorld/ScienceWorld).
limits: The pdftotext table layout is scrambled, so only headline figures are used here. No ablation of prune vs no-prune in ReMem; pruning rate is reported but its accuracy effect is not isolated. One run per cell, no intervals.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gaps 1 and 8: a non-agentic benchmark set, a different backbone family, equal retrieval budget. The retrieve-everything baseline (ExpRAG) is hard to beat on reasoning sets, so a pruning rule must be tested against it.

source: Weller et al. (2026) On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-Based Retrieval (ICLR 2026)
finding: A fixed embedding size caps how many different top-k document sets can be returned. In the best case with free vectors, the corpus size at which top-2 breaks is large. Real models fail earlier on the LIMIT test even with 50k simple documents.
numbers: Best-case critical corpus size for top-2: 500k docs (dim 512), 1.7M (768), 4M (1024), 107M (3072), 250M (4096), from a cubic fit with r2 0.999. LIMIT: 50k documents, 1000 queries, 2 relevant each. The small version (46 documents) still defeats all tested models at recall@10; BM25 drops nearly 90% on a harder variant.
limits: Tests recall of every top-k combination, not precision of nearest-neighbour in an ordinary case bank. Documents are artificial and very short.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a bank of tens of thousands of cases is far below the theoretical limit for dim >= 768, so any swamping at 10x-100x is more likely from similar-but-wrong neighbours than from lost capacity. Not a direct swamping measurement.

source: Gao et al. (2024) On the Noise Robustness of In-Context Learning for Text Generation (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: On generation tasks, wrong labels in the demonstration pool hurt in-context learning a lot, unlike classification. Better selectors (TopK, DPP) and more demonstrations make the harm worse. Replacing each selected candidate with a cleaner nearest neighbour picked by local perplexity (LPR) recovers much of the loss.
numbers: Llama-2-7B-Chat, 6 datasets, k=4 neighbours, threshold 50%. SciQ with 60% irrelevant label noise: TopK exact match 29.31 -> 48.06 with LPR (+18.75). NQ 60% noise: random selection 28.21 -> 42.00 (+13.79). Other models (Llama-2-13B, Mistral-7B, OPT-6.7B) also improve; average +7.83 EM at 60% noise on one model comparison.
limits: Small open models; noise made by pairing with unrelated outputs or ChatGPT-4 near-misses; not a delete-from-bank rule but a select-time filter. Performance with LPR is still below clean-label pool.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: cleaning wrong cases matters for generation-style banks, and the fix is local (compare a case with its near neighbours, drop the odd one out). That is the same idea as Delany-Cunningham editing, now with a measured gain.

source: Min et al. (2022) Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations: What Makes In-Context Learning Work?
finding: Replacing the labels of demonstrations with random labels barely hurts classification and multi-choice in-context learning over 12 models. What matters is the label space, the input text distribution and the format.
numbers: Drop 0-5% absolute; 2.6% on average for classification, 1.7% for multi-choice. k=16 demonstrations. Models up to GPT-3 175B.
limits: Short tasks with a small label set; Gao et al. (d06) show the opposite for generation. Models are 2022 era.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: label noise in a few-shot bank may cost little for classification, so cleaning effort should go to generation or reasoning banks, where Gao finds large harm. Case editing is not a general win.

source: Bertsch et al. (2024) In-Context Learning with Long-Context Models: An In-Depth Exploration
finding: As the number of in-context demonstrations grows into the hundreds or thousands, careful selection matters less. Retrieval beats random selection at short context but the gap shrinks with more examples.
numbers: 10 to 1000 demos: up to +50.8 points, average +36.8 over 5 datasets (Llama-2 80k). Banking-77: BM25 retrieval gain over random falls from 51.5 points at 1-shot to 4.9 at 1500-shot. In summarisation (SAMSum) retrieval sometimes did worse than random.
limits: Classification-heavy; Llama-2 variants with extended context; cost per query grows with demos (they note caching a fixed random set is cheaper).
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and 1: a large unpruned bank loaded wholesale costs tokens but selection quality stops mattering, so pruning has to be justified by cost, not accuracy. Cheaper fixed-set caching competes with per-query retrieval.

source: Fang et al. (2025) Memp: Exploring Agent Procedural Memory
finding: Tests three ways to update a procedural memory every t tasks: append everything (vanilla), keep only successful trajectories (validation, failures and noisy data discarded), and revise a retrieved memory in place when it led to a failure (adjustment, reflexion-style). All improve over no memory as groups of tasks pass; the in-place revision wins by the last group.
numbers: TravelPlanner and ALFWorld with GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Qwen2.5-72B. Reflexion-style adjustment beats the second-best update strategy by +0.7 reward and cuts 14 steps by the last group (Fig. 3, read from text). Retrieved-memory count: performance rises then plateaus, and retrieving too many lowers it. Memory built by GPT-4o moved to Qwen2.5-14B: +5% task completion, 1.6 fewer steps.
limits: Numbers are read from figures and short text; the append vs success-only gap is not given as a table value. Different agent family and three backbones, but still agent tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 8, 9, 6: a second agent family and a second set of backbones agree that update-in-place beats append, and that too many retrieved cases hurt. Failure handling here is revise-in-place, not drop.

source: Yan et al. (2025) Memory-R1: Enhancing LLM Agents to Manage and Utilize Memories via Reinforcement Learning
finding: A learned manager that picks ADD, UPDATE, DELETE or NOOP for each new fact beats a prompted (untrained) manager on long-conversation memory (LoCoMo, with transfer to MSC and LongMemEval). The untrained manager misreads additions as contradictions and issues DELETE+ADD, which fragments memory.
numbers: LLaMA-3.1-8B, PPO: F1/BLEU-1/judge 41.0/32.9/57.5 with trained manager vs 34.5/28.1/49.0 without. GRPO: 45.0/37.5/62.7 vs 37.5/30.6/52.9. Memory distillation (filter the 60 retrieved memories) adds +1.7 F1 under PPO (39.3 -> 41.0) and +4.0 under GRPO (41.0 -> 45.0). Pairing with a GPT-4o-mini manager raises the answer-agent gain from +10.10 to +19.72 F1.
limits: Conversation QA, not case reuse. Needs RL training and an answer-based reward, so it is not a scaffold-only result. Gains are against the same system with a prompted manager.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 7: the quality of the add/update/delete decision moves accuracy by 6 to 8 F1 points; a prompt-only manager that deletes wrongly is harmful. Agrees with Xiong that a bad retain judge costs points.

source: Gupta, Gardner, Singh (2023) Coverage-based Example Selection for In-Context Learning
finding: Ranking examples one by one by similarity picks redundant examples and misses parts of the test input. A set-level coverage score based on BERTScore-Recall (token-level embedding match) selects a set that covers the salient parts of the input.
numbers: 15 datasets, 6 tasks, 7 LLMs. BSR beats cosine by up to 8 points. For compositional tasks, set selection (SET-BSR) beats independent ranking by up to 17 points on average, and beats trained selectors on compositional splits (e.g. 61.2 vs 21.7 for EPR on one split).
limits: This is coverage of the test input at retrieval time, not coverage of the case bank as in Smyth and Keane. Gains are largest on compositional tasks and absent on IID splits.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: gives a workable embedding-based coverage definition (token-level soft match) but at query time. A bank-level 'coverage' could be defined by which queries a case would help to cover; this is not tested.

source: Su et al. (2022) Selective Annotation Makes Language Models Better Few-Shot Learners (vote-k)
finding: Choosing which examples enter the pool by diversity and representativeness (graph-based vote-k) beats random choice, and makes results more stable.
numbers: 10 datasets. Relative gain over random pool selection: 12.9% with 18 annotated examples, 11.4% with 100 (5.2 points absolute at 100). Reaches finetuning-level results with 10x-100x less annotation.
limits: Pool selection before labelling, from an unlabeled set, Codex-era models. Does not test pruning an existing bank.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a diversity-based keep rule, using only embeddings, works for pool building. This is the nearest tested analogue to Smyth-Keane 'keep pivotal, drop support' for LLM banks.

source: Xu et al. (2025) A-Mem: Agentic Memory for LLM Agents
finding: Memory notes are linked to neighbours (link generation, LG) and neighbours are rewritten as new notes arrive (memory evolution, ME). Removing both is very costly; removing only ME also costs. Nothing is deleted. Retrieval latency stays low as memory grows to 1M notes.
numbers: LoCoMo with GPT-4o-mini F1: multi-hop 27.02 (full), 21.35 (w/o ME), 9.65 (w/o LG and ME); temporal 45.85/31.24/24.55; adversarial 50.03/44.16/15.32. Retrieval time A-Mem 0.31 us at 1k notes to 3.70 us at 1M. The baseline MemoryBank row rises 43.6 us -> 120,070 us over the same range (table row labels are ambiguous in pdftotext).
limits: Latency only, not precision at scale. Accuracy at 1M notes was not measured. The 'memory evolution' step is closer to merging than deleting.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and 7: cost does not blow up at 10x-1000x size with a vector index, so size pressure on a case bank is about accuracy (wrong neighbours), not speed. Updating neighbours on insert helps accuracy more than appending.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), appendix A.5-A.6
finding: ACE merges and de-duplicates new insights into a running playbook by non-LLM similarity, and prunes when it gets long. The paper tests the dedup threshold and the pruning trigger on FiNER (financial entity tagging, not an agent task) with DeepSeek-V3.1.
numbers: Base accuracy 70.7. Dedup threshold 50% -> 77.0, 70% -> 73.9, 90% -> 78.6. Pruning trigger at 10K, 50K, 100K tokens -> 78.6, 78.4, 78.3. Reflection rounds on AppWorld 1/3/5/10: average 61.3/65.8/67.6/65.2. Incremental updates vs none on AppWorld average: 70.3 vs 56.9 (base 53.3).
limits: Single run per setting, no intervals; the 70% dip (-4.7 vs 90%) is as large as the claimed gain from dedup, so dedup effect is not distinguishable from noise. There is no no-dedup arm and no no-pruning arm, only different thresholds.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 and 1: on a non-agentic benchmark a pruned context at 10K tokens matches one allowed to grow to 100K, so a small cap loses nothing here. Dedup aggressiveness changes accuracy little; its main use is cost. Still no clean dedup on/off test.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) SAGE: Self-evolving Agents with Reflective and Memory-augmented Abilities (Table 5)
finding: A MemoryBank-style Ebbinghaus forgetting-curve optimiser is used inside a self-evolving agent. The only ablation compares agents with and without the whole memory optimisation, not forgetting vs no forgetting.
numbers: AgentBench, Qwen-1.8B: with memory vs without: OS 18.7 vs 10.4, DB 28.3 vs 22.6, KG 45.3 vs 6.8, ALF 10.5 vs 0.0. CodeLlama-7B: DB 41.3 vs 2.7, WS 58.7 vs 14.3.
limits: Compares memory against no memory. It cannot show whether decay-based deletion helps. Tiny models.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open: second paper to adopt Ebbinghaus decay without isolating it.

source: Kang et al. (2025) Memory OS of AI Agent (MemoryOS)
finding: Memory segments get a heat score from visit count, interaction length and recency. When the mid-term store is full, the lowest-heat segments are evicted. Ablations remove the mid-term store, the persona module, the dialogue chain, or the whole system.
numbers: LoCoMo with GPT-4o-mini: average gain over the best baseline +49.11% F1 and +46.18% BLEU-1 (abstract). Capacity set to 100 entries with a heat threshold.
limits: No ablation replaces heat-based eviction with recency or FIFO eviction, so the usage-based rule itself is untested.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open: usage-based eviction is in production style systems but has no head-to-head against recency in the papers read.

source: Wang et al. (2023) MemoryBank, contributions list and forgetting section
finding: Re-read: the paper says it shows 'applicability with and without memory forgetting mechanism', meaning the system runs either way. It reports no accuracy comparison of forgetting vs not.
numbers: No ablation table on forgetting. Forgetting rule: retention R = exp(-t/S), strength S +1 and t reset on recall.
limits: Evaluation is qualitative plus a small human-rated study of a companion bot.
agent_relevance: Confirms claim K22: Ebbinghaus-style forgetting is still not shown to help.

source: Pan et al. (2024) Autonomous Evaluation and Refinement of Digital Agents (COLM 2024)
finding: Model judges of agent trajectories are good enough to be used as filters. Judge accuracy against oracle checks was 74 to 93%, and using them to refine policies gave large gains.
numbers: WebArena accuracy vs oracle: GPT-4V end-to-end 80.6, Captioner+Mixtral 74.4, Captioner+GPT-4 82.1, Qwen-VL 68.0. Android: 90.6 / 92.9 / 89.8 / 70.2. Judges improve WebArena agent by up to 29% relative (inference-time guidance) and iOS by about 75% relative (filtered behaviour cloning).
limits: Judge and agent are different from Xiong's setup; gains were measured against an unfiltered baseline, not against a fixed-size memory.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: judges of 75-90% accuracy already give a big gain when used as a filter. That sides with ReasoningBank (judge accuracy does not matter much) for web-style tasks. Xiong's coarse judges were evaluators of a different sort.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: A model asked to judge and fix its own answer without an outside label gets worse. With oracle labels it looks good, but that is not self-correction. The model cannot reliably tell when its own reasoning is right.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K: 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7 after two self-correction rounds; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8. With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3, GPT-4 97.5 (table layout partly garbled). For GSM8K, GPT-3.5 keeps its first answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: Tests self-correction, not retain decisions. Prompted self-judging only, on 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a same-model judge on reasoning tasks may be near chance for retain decisions, unlike the verifier-backed or outcome-backed judges used on web and code. Ground-truth outcome should gate retention where available.

source: Agarwal et al. (2024) Many-Shot In-Context Learning, flipped-label analysis
finding: With many shots, models learn to follow even flipped or abstract labels, approaching default-label performance. Early confidence drops then rises sharply. Large banks of examples can overwrite the model's priors.
numbers: Figure caption on sentiment: flipped and abstract labels approach default-label performance as shots increase (no exact figure copied).
limits: Labels are flipped consistently, not randomly wrong; it tests learning of a new mapping, not tolerance of noise.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 side note: a large consistent error in the bank is learned, random error is mostly ignored (compare Min). Systematic errors are the dangerous kind.
